hook.text: Americans say 'passed away.' Mexicans throw parties for the dead. Comfort levels vary wildly.

buildup.text: English has dozens of euphemisms for dying. 'Lost,' 'departed,' 'at peace'—we circle the word.

discovery.text: In Bhutan, people meditate on death five times daily. They rank among the world's happiest.

twist.text: Victorian England was obsessed with death rituals but terrified of saying the word. Contradiction built in.

climax.text: Cultures that avoid death talk don't fear it less. They just hide the fear differently.

punchline.text: The words we dodge reveal our deepest fears.

quiz.question: In Bhutan, how often are people encouraged to think about death daily?

details.summary: Western cultures often treat death as the ultimate conversational taboo, using euphemisms like 'passed away' or 'lost.' Many non-Western cultures discuss death openly — Mexican Día de los Muertos celebrates the dead with parties, while Buddhists meditate on death daily.
details.whyItMatters: Death avoidance in Western culture contributes to poor end-of-life planning and grief isolation. Cultures that discuss death openly often handle bereavement more healthily.
takeaways: Western cultures use extensive euphemisms to avoid saying 'death'
Many non-Western cultures treat death as a normal conversation topic
The death positive movement advocates for open discussion of mortality

faq.question: Why is death taboo in Western culture?
faq.answer: Western death avoidance grew from the medicalization of death (moving dying from homes to hospitals), increasing secularism (reducing religious frameworks for death), and consumer culture's emphasis on youth and vitality.

faq.question: Which cultures are most open about death?
faq.answer: Mexican culture celebrates Día de los Muertos with altars and parties honoring dead relatives. Tibetan Buddhists meditate on death daily as spiritual practice. Ghanaian fantasy coffins celebrate the deceased's life. Indonesian Toraja people keep mummified relatives at home for years.
